source.title: The effect of fatigue on peak strain of hamstring muscles in dominant and non-dominant sides during sprinting: a pre-post intervention study

paper.citation: Liu Y., Li Q., Yang C., Wan X. The effect of fatigue on peak strain of hamstring muscles in dominant and non-dominant sides during sprinting: a pre-post intervention study. BMC Musculoskeletal Disorders. 2026;27(1):305. doi:10.1186/s12891-026-09699-9.
paper.abstract: This paper addresses the following question: Does an acute intermittent-running fatigue protocol alter modeled optimal length, peak length, and peak strain of the biarticular hamstrings during sprinting, and do those changes differ between dominant and non-dominant limbs? Nineteen male, high-national-level track-and-field athletes aged 18 to 25 years participated; mean age was 19.2 years, and all had 100-m personal bests of 11.74 seconds or faster. None reported a hamstring strain in the prior two years or a significant lower-limb or foot injury in the prior six months. This was a single-group pre-post laboratory intervention. Participants completed maximal 40-m sprint trials, isokinetic knee-flexion testing, and a modified Loughborough Intermittent Shuttle Test individualized from VO2max, followed by repeated testing.
paper.tldr: Maximal hamstring strength decreased after the fatigue protocol in both limbs, supporting that the protocol induced an acute loss of force-generating capacity. Modeled optimal length shortened after fatigue for all three biarticular hamstrings in the non-dominant limb, with large within-limb effects, whereas changes in the dominant limb were not statistically significant. Treat the results as a reason to preserve sprint quality and account for fatigue exposure, not as evidence that the non-dominant limb is categorically at greater injury risk.
paper.methods: This was a single-group pre-post laboratory intervention. Participants completed maximal 40-m sprint trials, isokinetic knee-flexion testing, and a modified Loughborough Intermittent Shuttle Test individualized from VO2max, followed by repeated testing. Three-dimensional motion capture, force platforms, and a musculoskeletal model estimated optimal muscle length, sprint-phase peak muscle length, and strain for biceps femoris long head, semimembranosus, and semitendinosus. Strain was calculated relative to the modeled optimal length; paired tests and repeated-measures ANCOVA examined time and limb effects.
paper.findings: Maximal hamstring strength decreased after the fatigue protocol in both limbs, supporting that the protocol induced an acute loss of force-generating capacity. Modeled optimal length shortened after fatigue for all three biarticular hamstrings in the non-dominant limb, with large within-limb effects, whereas changes in the dominant limb were not statistically significant. Peak absolute hamstring length and maximal hip-knee angle during sprinting did not change significantly after fatigue in either limb. Peak modeled strain increased in the non-dominant biceps femoris long head and semimembranosus, but not significantly in the dominant limb or non-dominant semitendinosus. Despite the within-limb findings, changes in peak strain did not differ significantly between limbs, and adjustment for baseline strength removed the apparent between-limb contrast. Peak strain continued to occur in late swing, approximately 85% to 95% of the gait cycle, and fatigue did not significantly change its timing.
paper.limitations: The sample was small, male-only, and limited to trained track athletes; estimated post-hoc power was no greater than 0.64 for subtle effects. There was no non-fatigued control condition, so time, repeated maximal sprints, modeling, or order-related influences cannot be fully separated from the intervention. The fatigue protocol may not reproduce American football practice or game fatigue, dominance was defined by ball striking in sprinters, and muscle behavior was modeled from surface-marker kinematics and isokinetic testing rather than measured at fascicle level. Neuromuscular activation was not recorded. The study measured acute biomechanical surrogates, not hamstring injuries, so it cannot establish that the observed strain changes cause injury or justify a screening threshold.
paper.practicalImplications: Treat the results as a reason to preserve sprint quality and account for fatigue exposure, not as evidence that the non-dominant limb is categorically at greater injury risk. In collegiate American football, monitor within-athlete sprint mechanics, strength capacity, exposure, and symptoms across realistic practice demands; do not infer injury probability from modeled strain or a single asymmetry. Where a meaningful and repeatable limb difference is present, investigate whether unequal strength or relative loading contributes, but keep decisions within a multifactorial hamstring-risk framework.
